name: iRestore Hair Growth System

card.summary: A helmet-style red-light (low-level laser) device worn at home on the scalp, intended to thicken thinning hair for a fuller-looking head of hair.
card.note: Results depend on continued use; long-term effects are not known.

quick.overview:
The iRestore is a laser or red-light helmet worn over the scalp at home. It belongs to the low-level laser therapy category used for pattern hair loss.

Users hope for thicker, denser hair. Reviews of low-level laser devices generally report improved hair density versus baseline or sham in many trials, though reviewers call for larger, longer, blinded studies.
quick.how: The user wears the helmet for short scheduled sessions several times a week, often alongside minoxidil or finasteride, and tracks results over many months.
quick.risks: Reported effects are mild scalp irritation or discomfort. Long-term effects are unknown. Dermatologist input is suggested before starting, and users on forums note cost.

lead: The iRestore Hair Growth System is a family of home-use laser helmets, sold as the Elite (500 diodes), Professional (282) and Essential (120), marketed as FDA-cleared red light therapy devices.[1] Bundles were listed at $1,797 (Professional) and $2,797 (Elite).[1]

Low-level laser therapy for hair is thought to work when light is absorbed by cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria; hat, comb and helmet formats exist.[2] A 2017 review reported 10 of 11 trials showing significant improvement in androgenetic alopecia, while earlier reviews in 2012-2015 were mixed, and larger blinded trials are called for.[2]
On T Nation, one poster asked whether the new iRestore helmet could help hair loss in someone on TRT.[3]

chain: Possible increase in hair density over months
angle.text: Users wear it to try to thicken thinning hair at the crown and top. Benefit depends on continued use.

paras: The three models differ mainly in diode count: 500, 282 and 120.[1]

Reviews of laser hair devices in general report increased density in both sexes, with red and infrared light favoured for androgenetic alopecia, and device type and treatment duration not clearly altering effect.[2]

Some users report mild pain or skin irritation, long-term effects are unknown, and dermatologist consultation is suggested.[2] In 2015 the FDA obtained an injunction against QLaser over broad disease claims, a different company.[2]
No studies found specific to this product in cited sources. Wikipedia's low-level laser therapy article summarises category-level trials and reviews as above.[2]

lore.intro: Hair-loss forum users ask about laser helmets as an add-on to standard treatments.[3]

claims.claim: A laser helmet can help hair even with high DHT
claims.believers: A T Nation poster asked about the new iRestore helmet for hair loss on TRT, noting it might work even with elevated DHT.[3]
claims.experts: Category-level reviews report improvements in density but call for larger trials.[2]
